claim: Channel age does not distinguish successful YouTube creators from unsuccessful ones - average days active is roughly constant across subscriber tiers - while output volume does: elite channels average 940 published videos against 294 for the tier below.
stance_target: Creator success is primarily a function of time spent on the platform
scope_conditions: 36,336,861 channels crawled 2019-2020, of which 4,415,180 have over 1,000 subscribers; 'days active since the starting date' is a crude tenure proxy and the sub-1,000-subscriber stratum is acknowledged as unreliable
quoted_support: the elite may receive disproportionate levels of exposure but have also published, on average, many more videos per channel (940) than the next lower tier (294). And this is not simply an effect of having been around for a longer time: if we compare the average number of days active since the starting date, the numbers are surprisingly constant between tiers.
numbers: days active roughly constant across all four tiers

claim: The 153,000 YouTube channels above 100,000 subscribers are 0.42% of the platform yet take 69.2% of subscribers and 62.4% of views while producing only 8.9% of videos - a far heavier skew than the Pareto 80/20 rule.
stance_target: Creator platforms concentrate reward far beyond ordinary market inequality
scope_conditions: Crawl of 36,336,861 channels, 2019-2020; the sub-1,000-subscriber stratum (about 32 million channels) is the least reliable part of the sample, which if anything understates concentration
quoted_support: the 153k elite channels above 100k subscribers, a mere 0.42 percent of our total sample, account for 69.2 percent of subscribers and 62.4 percent of views.

claim: The 15,496 YouTube channels above one million subscribers - 0.04% of the platform - take 37% of subscribers and 37.4% of views while producing 2.3% of videos.
stance_target: Reward concentration continues without limit into the extreme top tail
quoted_support: looking at the 15,496 channels that have more than 1M subscribers (0,04 percent), we found that they account for 37 percent of the subscribers, 37.4 percent of the views, but only 2.3 percent of the videos published. This is a much heavier skew than the 80/20 Pareto principle

claim: More than half of all videos published by YouTube's 4.4 million monetizable channels fail to reach 550 views, even with elite channels included in that sample.
stance_target: The typical unit of creator output receives almost no audience
scope_conditions: Videos from the 4,415,180 channels with at least 1,000 subscribers - i.e. only channels ALREADY past the monetization threshold; the true median across all channels would be lower
quoted_support: More than half of the videos published fail to reach 550 views, despite the elite being included in this sample.
numbers: over 25% of videos are under two minutes

claim: YouTube's advertising monetization is gated at 1,000 subscribers, and channels below that threshold - roughly 32 million of the 36.3 million discovered, averaging 122 subscribers - are structurally excluded from earning anything.
stance_target: Zero earnings for most creators is a designed platform property, not a market outcome
scope_conditions: Describes YouTube's tier system as of 2020; the sub-1,000 stratum is the least reliably crawled part of the dataset
quoted_support: passing the threshold of 1,000 subscribers awards ‘opal’ credentials and, more importantly, access to monetization through advertisement ... This is particularly visible if we move below the monetization threshold, where the average subscriber number drops to 122.

claim: Indonesian and Brazilian YouTube channels achieve far fewer views than their share of channels would predict, while Thai channels achieve unusually high average views per channel - so Southeast Asian creator outcomes diverge sharply from each other and from the US pattern.
stance_target: Creator-economy outcomes are uniform across countries
scope_conditions: Based on creator-selected country flags in the elite (100k+ subscriber) tier; in the full 4.4 million monetizable channel set, 53.6% of channels have no country set at all, so all country analysis covers under half the platform
quoted_support: Countries like Brazil and Indonesia stand out for achieving far fewer views than their overall share of channels would suggest. ... Thailand and Turkey (TR) also stand out with a high level of average views per channel, which signals strong uptake of YouTube in their respective locales.
numbers: 53.6% of monetizable channels have no country set
region: Cross-country; explicitly covers Indonesia, Thailand and Vietnam

claim: English-language creators convert less output into more reward: the US and Great Britain achieve higher subscriber and view counts with fewer videos, while India, South Korea and Egypt publish disproportionately many videos for their returns.
stance_target: Language and market position, not effort, determine creator returns per unit of work
scope_conditions: Elite tier (100k+ subscribers) only, creator-selected country flags; South Korea is a partial exception because K-pop converts output into international views
quoted_support: the US is ‘punching above its weight’ in terms of subscribers and views, achieving greater success with fewer videos published. Only Great Britain achieves a similar feat, pointing toward the crucial advantage the English language confers.
region: Cross-country comparison in the elite tier

claim: Channel metadata quality decays systematically going down the subscriber tiers, so any research method that relies on channel metadata under-observes exactly the small creators whose outcomes are in question.
stance_target: Measurement bias in creator research compounds survivorship bias
scope_conditions: Observed across the four subscriber tiers in the 36.3-million-channel crawl; the authors also state their own sub-1,000-subscriber data must be treated with the most caution
quoted_support: The decay in metadata quality again resonates with the idea that the elite invests more heavily in [metadata optimization]
numbers: 10-15% of 1k-10k channels estimated missing from the crawl
